rows.sourceTitle: Comparison of holmium laser enucleation and transurethral resection of prostate in benign prostatic hyperplasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
rows.sourceDesign: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
rows.scopeFinding: The meta-analysis directly evaluates TURP and HoLEP performed for BPH and reports postoperative urethral stricture as an adverse event; HoLEP had a significantly lower stricture risk than TURP. This supports a treatment-mediated post-procedure stricture pathway, not a claim that untreated BPH itself causes stricture.
rows.implementationProposition: Treatment-mediated urethral-stricture risk after TURP or HoLEP performed for documented benign prostatic hyperplasia.
rows.finalProposition: Treatment-mediated urethral-stricture risk after TURP or HoLEP performed for documented benign prostatic hyperplasia.
rows.implementationGuard: Require documented benign prostatic hyperplasia, documented transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) or holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP), and a separately established urethral stricture arising after that procedure with compatible chronology. Do not infer urethral stricture from untreated BPH, lower urinary tract symptoms, or bladder-outlet obstruction alone. Preserve prior urethral instrumentation or trauma, infection, lichen sclerosus, prior pelvic surgery or radiation, and other recognized causes of urethral stricture.
rows.finalGuard: Require documented benign prostatic hyperplasia, documented transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) or holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP), and a separately established urethral stricture arising after that procedure with compatible chronology. Do not infer urethral stricture from untreated BPH, lower urinary tract symptoms, or bladder-outlet obstruction alone. Preserve prior urethral instrumentation or trauma, infection, lichen sclerosus, prior pelvic surgery or radiation, and other recognized causes of urethral stricture.
rows.implementationCitation: Chen F, Chen Y, Zou Y, Wang Y, Wu X, Chen M. Comparison of holmium laser enucleation and transurethral resection of prostate in benign prostatic hyperplasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Int Med Res. 2023;51(8):3000605231190763. PMID 37561537. doi:10.1177/03000605231190763.
rows.finalCitation: Chen F, Chen Y, Zou Y, Wang Y, Wu X, Chen M. Comparison of holmium laser enucleation and transurethral resection of prostate in benign prostatic hyperplasia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Int Med Res. 2023;51(8):3000605231190763. PMID 37561537. doi:10.1177/03000605231190763.
rows.implementationPhenotypeRestriction: treatment-related urethral stricture after TURP or HoLEP for BPH
rows.finalPhenotypeRestriction: treatment-related urethral stricture after TURP or HoLEP for BPH

rows.sourceTitle: Q fever in Spain: Description of a new series, and systematic review
rows.scopeFinding: The systematic review reports hepatitis as a recognized presentation of Q fever (31% overall in the reviewed Spanish series, with regional variation). It supports acute Q-fever-associated hepatitis. It does not independently validate a broader generic 'hepatic injury' phenotype or isolated nonspecific transaminase elevation.
rows.implementationProposition: Acute Q-fever-associated hepatitis or hepatic injury as a recognized acute manifestation/complication.
rows.finalProposition: Acute hepatitis as a recognized clinical manifestation of acute Q fever.
rows.implementationGuard: Require clinically established acute Q fever using appropriate Coxiella burnetii diagnostic evidence and separately established acute hepatitis or hepatic injury with compatible timing. Do not generalize this edge to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or an isolated nonspecific liver-enzyme elevation without a compatible acute Q-fever syndrome. Preserve viral hepatitis, alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, drug- or toxin-induced injury, ischemic injury, biliary disease, and other hepatic causes.
rows.finalGuard: Require clinically established acute Q fever using appropriate Coxiella burnetii diagnostic evidence and separately established acute hepatitis with compatible timing. Do not generalize this edge to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or an isolated nonspecific liver-enzyme elevation without a compatible acute Q-fever syndrome. Preserve viral hepatitis, alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, drug- or toxin-induced injury, ischemic injury, biliary disease, and other hepatic causes.
rows.implementationCitation: Alende-Castro V, Macía-Rodríguez C, Novo-Veleiro I, et al. Q fever in Spain: Description of a new series, and systematic review. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2018;12(3):e0006338. PMID 29543806. doi:10.1371/journal.pntd.0006338.
rows.finalCitation: Alende-Castro V, Macía-Rodríguez C, Novo-Veleiro I, et al. Q fever in Spain: Description of a new series, and systematic review. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2018;12(3):e0006338. PMID 29543806. doi:10.1371/journal.pntd.0006338.

rows.sourceTitle: Clinical Phenotype and Outcomes of Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Myeloproliferative Neoplasms: A Population-based Study
rows.scopeFinding: The registry includes 90 patients with myeloproliferative neoplasms and precapillary pulmonary hypertension, including 42 with polycythemia vera. Half had CTEPH and half group-5 PH; PV and essential thrombocythemia were generally related to CTEPH. The source is phenotype-specific to precapillary PH and does not support generic/postcapillary PH.
rows.implementationProposition: Hemodynamically established pulmonary hypertension associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms, including PV-associated CTEPH/group-5 phenotypes.
rows.finalProposition: Hemodynamically established precapillary pulmonary hypertension can occur with myeloproliferative neoplasms; in polycythemia vera the registry evidence is strongest for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, while group-5 PH is also represented across the MPN cohort.
rows.implementationGuard: Require confirmed polycythemia vera and a separately established pulmonary-hypertension diagnosis using appropriate hemodynamic evaluation, with classification of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension versus group-5 or other PH mechanisms. Do not infer pulmonary hypertension from polycythemia vera, dyspnea, hypoxemia, or an isolated echocardiographic estimate alone. Treat the registry as population-level complication evidence rather than automatic individual causation. Preserve left-heart disease, chronic lung disease or hypoxia, sleep-disordered breathing, unrelated thromboembolic disease, medications, and other recognized pulmonary-hypertension causes.
rows.finalGuard: Require confirmed polycythemia vera and separately established precapillary pulmonary hypertension using appropriate hemodynamic evaluation, with classification of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension versus group-5 PH when applicable. The source is strongest for CTEPH in polycythemia vera/essential thrombocythemia and does not support postcapillary pulmonary hypertension caused by left-heart disease. Do not infer pulmonary hypertension from polycythemia vera, dyspnea, hypoxemia, or an isolated echocardiographic estimate alone. Treat the registry as population-level complication evidence rather than automatic individual causation. Preserve left-heart disease, chronic lung disease or hypoxia, sleep-disordered breathing, unrelated thromboembolic disease, medications, and other recognized pulmonary-hypertension causes.
rows.implementationCitation: Montani D, Thoré P, Mignard X, et al. Clinical Phenotype and Outcomes of Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Myeloproliferative Neoplasms: A Population-based Study. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2023;208(5):600-612. PMID 37311222. doi:10.1164/rccm.202210-1941OC.
rows.finalCitation: Montani D, Thoré P, Mignard X, et al. Clinical Phenotype and Outcomes of Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Myeloproliferative Neoplasms: A Population-based Study. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2023;208(5):600-612. PMID 37311222. doi:10.1164/rccm.202210-1941OC.
rows.implementationPhenotypeRestriction: hemodynamically confirmed MPN-associated precapillary PH, including CTEPH or group-5 PH
rows.finalPhenotypeRestriction: hemodynamically confirmed precapillary PH, with CTEPH versus group-5 classification when applicable

rows.sourceTitle: Role of the lower esophageal sphincter and hiatal hernia in the pathogenesis of gastroesophageal reflux disease
rows.sourceDesign: clinical physiologic cohort with multivariable analysis
rows.scopeFinding: In 375 symptomatic patients without prior foregut surgery, hiatal hernia and a structurally defective lower esophageal sphincter were independent predictors of abnormal esophageal acid exposure. The source supports hiatal hernia as an anatomic contributor to objectively established GERD and does not imply that every hiatal hernia produces GERD.
rows.implementationProposition: Physiologically relevant hiatal hernia as an anatomic contributor to objectively established gastroesophageal reflux disease.
rows.finalProposition: Physiologically relevant hiatal hernia as an anatomic contributor to objectively established gastroesophageal reflux disease.
rows.implementationGuard: Require a documented hiatal hernia, with the source proposition most directly applicable to a sliding or otherwise physiologically relevant gastroesophageal-junction hernia, and a separately established diagnosis of GERD using appropriate clinical, endoscopic, or reflux-monitoring evidence. Do not infer GERD solely from the presence of a hiatal hernia. Preserve lower-esophageal-sphincter dysfunction, obesity, medications, delayed gastric emptying, dietary or behavioral contributors, prior foregut surgery, and other reflux causes.
rows.finalGuard: Require a documented hiatal hernia, with the source proposition most directly applicable to a sliding or otherwise physiologically relevant gastroesophageal-junction hernia, and a separately established diagnosis of GERD using appropriate clinical, endoscopic, or reflux-monitoring evidence. Do not infer GERD solely from the presence of a hiatal hernia. Preserve lower-esophageal-sphincter dysfunction, obesity, medications, delayed gastric emptying, dietary or behavioral contributors, prior foregut surgery, and other reflux causes.
rows.implementationCitation: Fein M, Ritter MP, DeMeester TR, et al. Role of the lower esophageal sphincter and hiatal hernia in the pathogenesis of gastroesophageal reflux disease. J Gastrointest Surg. 1999;3(4):405-410. PMID 10482693. doi:10.1016/S1091-255X(99)80057-2.
rows.finalCitation: Fein M, Ritter MP, DeMeester TR, et al. Role of the lower esophageal sphincter and hiatal hernia in the pathogenesis of gastroesophageal reflux disease. J Gastrointest Surg. 1999;3(4):405-410. PMID 10482693. doi:10.1016/S1091-255X(99)80057-2.
rows.implementationPhenotypeRestriction: physiologically relevant/sliding hiatal hernia with separately established GERD
rows.finalPhenotypeRestriction: physiologically relevant/sliding hiatal hernia with separately established GERD

rows.sourceTitle: Reduction in myocardial function and oxygen consumption after chemoradiotherapy in patients with esophageal cancer
rows.scopeFinding: The prospective study measured 47 esophageal-cancer patients before and immediately after chemoradiotherapy and found statistically significant early reductions in GLS and LVEF, with 21% showing specified absolute decreases. It supports early treatment-related LV dysfunction/cardiotoxicity. The study does not establish a clinical cardiomyopathy diagnosis or prove individual causation. The implementation citation also truncates compound surnames; the same PMID/DOI should be retained while the author string is corrected.
rows.implementationCitation: Søndergaard MMA, Nordsmark M, Møller DS, Nielsen KM, Poulsen SH. Reduction in myocardial function and oxygen consumption after chemoradiotherapy in patients with esophageal cancer. Acta Oncol. 2022;61(5):566-574. PMID 35289694. doi:10.1080/0284186X.2022.2048068.
rows.finalCitation: Astrup Søndergaard MM, Nordsmark M, Sloth Møller D, Melgaard Nielsen K, Poulsen SH. Reduction in myocardial function and oxygen consumption after chemoradiotherapy in patients with esophageal cancer. Acta Oncol. 2022;61(5):566-574. PMID 35289694. doi:10.1080/0284186X.2022.2048068.
rows.implementationProposition: Treatment-mediated myocardial dysfunction/cardiomyopathy following actual thoracic chemoradiotherapy for esophageal cancer.
rows.finalProposition: Thoracic chemoradiotherapy for esophageal cancer is associated with early left-ventricular functional decline; this source supports a treatment-mediated cardiotoxicity pathway but does not by itself establish cardiomyopathy.
rows.implementationGuard: Require documented esophageal cancer, actual exposure to thoracic chemoradiotherapy, and a separately established myocardial-dysfunction or cardiomyopathy phenotype with compatible post-treatment chronology. Do not infer cardiomyopathy from the cancer diagnosis, radiation exposure, a small isolated strain change, fatigue, or dyspnea alone. Preserve pre-existing cardiomyopathy or heart failure, ischemic disease, hypertension, valvular disease, arrhythmia, other cardiotoxic therapies, alcohol or toxin exposure, genetic cardiomyopathy, and other recognized myocardial causes.
rows.finalGuard: Require documented esophageal cancer, actual exposure to thoracic chemoradiotherapy, and a separately established cardiomyopathy diagnosis with compatible post-treatment chronology. Use this source only as evidence that chemoradiotherapy can produce early left-ventricular dysfunction/cardiotoxicity; it does not itself establish cardiomyopathy or individual causation. Do not infer cardiomyopathy from the cancer diagnosis, radiation exposure, a small isolated strain or ejection-fraction change, fatigue, or dyspnea alone. Preserve pre-existing cardiomyopathy or heart failure, ischemic disease, hypertension, valvular disease, arrhythmia, other cardiotoxic therapies, alcohol or toxin exposure, genetic cardiomyopathy, and other recognized myocardial causes.
rows.implementationPhenotypeRestriction: treatment-related myocardial dysfunction/cardiomyopathy after esophageal-cancer chemoradiotherapy
rows.finalPhenotypeRestriction: separately established cardiomyopathy after thoracic chemoradiotherapy for esophageal cancer
